analysis.one_liner: Bans charging excessively inflated prices for essentials during declared emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee; no committee vote, floor vote, or hearing ever happened, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During a declared disaster or public health emergency, the bill would make it illegal to sell essential goods at prices more than 10% above their average over the 120 days before the emergency, unless the seller proves higher costs justify the increase. It covers food, water, medicine, gasoline, and protective equipment, and gives both the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general power to enforce it. Introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic, it never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People shopping during emergencies, when essentials like masks, hand sanitizer, food, water, medicine, and gasoline are suddenly in short supply and prices can spike. The bill sets a clear line, presuming any price more than 10% above the pre-emergency average is excessive unless the seller proves the increase came from its own higher costs. It lets state attorneys general sue in federal or state court to stop the practice, impose penalties, and win restitution for their residents, so enforcement does not depend only on federal action.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers of essential goods during emergencies

how_it_helps.text: Presumes any price over 10% above the 120-day pre-emergency average is excessive or opportunistic, shifting the burden to the seller to prove higher procurement costs justify it.

Covers essentials people cannot skip during a crisis: food, water, gasoline, prescription and over-the-counter medications, and personal protective equipment, plus anything public health officials deem vital.

Gives the Federal Trade Commission enforcement authority treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and lets state attorneys general sue for injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for residents.
Applies during declared major disasters and public health emergencies, plus the 30 days after the declaration ends, covering the period when shortages and price spikes persist.

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essential consumer goods, including retailers, pharmacies, gas stations, and online resellers, who would face a presumption of liability for any emergency-period price more than 10% above the pre-emergency average and could owe penalties and restitution if they cannot document that their own costs rose.

drawbacks.text: A bright 10% presumption is crude: legitimate cost swings in disrupted supply chains can exceed it, and a seller must rebut the presumption by clear and convincing evidence, a demanding standard that could chill price adjustments even when justified.

Business groups generally oppose federal price-gouging rules as duplicating state laws that already exist in most states, arguing federal standards add litigation risk without protecting consumers any better; such arguments are standard in debates over these bills, though no group testimony on this bill appears in the record.

An average-price benchmark can misfire when the pre-emergency baseline itself is unusual, either masking gouging that began before a formal declaration or penalizing honest repricing after a declaration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the protection is straightforward: it targets only declared emergencies, applies to goods people cannot do without, and lets sellers escape liability by proving genuine cost increases, so honest retailers have a clear path out. The main cost falls on sellers facing a low 10% threshold and a demanding rebuttal standard, which risks some litigation over legitimate price changes. On balance the bill is a modest, targeted consumer protection, not a sweeping price control; its practical effect would have depended heavily on aggressive enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Warren introduced the bill on June 1, 2020, during the COVID-19 public health emergency, with Harris as its only cosponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, the only action the Senate ever took on it.
The committee scheduled no markup or hearing, no version passed either chamber, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of essentials avoided any federal price-gouging presumption or penalty during the rest of the pandemic; shoppers remained protected only by the varying price-gouging laws some states already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Essential-goods sellers; consumers kept only state protections

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred: no hearing, no markup, no vote, before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor joined, but there were no votes or floor debate, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Retailers and resellers of essential goods (grocery, pharmacy, gas, e-commerce)
industries.note: The bill would have created a legal presumption that emergency prices over 10% above the prior average are unlawful, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement, penalties, and restitution. That exposure is exactly what sellers of masks, sanitizer, food, and gasoline avoided when the bill died.
